title: Meditations close

segments.voice: Yesterday: your own notebook, Marcus writing to the one reader who needed it most. Your line was to myself. Did you add a fourth line last night? Day six hundred forty.

Day five hundred twenty-one, we opened a notebook kept by a Roman emperor and started reading it in order, which most people never do. They dip in, find a line for a mug, close it again. We went the long way: twelve books, a hundred and twenty days, the dull pages along with the famous ones. Today the notebook closes. Not with a test. With a question Marcus would ask: what will you actually do with it now? Today: the Meditations, closed.
screen: `DAY 521: THE NOTEBOOK OPENS.` → `TWELVE BOOKS, THE LONG WAY.` → `THE NOTEBOOK CLOSES.`

segments.voice: First, look back at the road. Book one is all thank-yous: to his grandfather, his mother, his teachers, his adoptive father, one by one, for what each taught him. Then book two opens with a morning warning: today you'll meet people who are rude, ungrateful, dishonest; they're kin; don't be harmed. From there the notebook wanders and circles: retreat into yourself; get up and do your work; all is opinion; the view from above; Alexander and his mule driver; and finally, in book twelve, two gates, a small share of time, and an actor leaving the stage at peace. Second, what reading straight through gives you. The famous lines sit in context. You see Marcus repeat himself, contradict himself, fall short, try again. You meet a person, not a quote generator. Third, the Greek word for reading. Anagignōskō: literally, to know again, to recognize. In Greek, to read is already to know a second time. That fits this book better than most. Marcus wasn't learning new things in it. He was recognizing old ones, again. Fourth, what readers do now. Many people who finish the Meditations start over. Some keep a single page open for a season. Some read one passage every morning, the way Marcus told himself to prepare for the day. There's no wrong way, except treating it as finished. Tomorrow the path widens: the Stoics who came before Marcus, the neighbors who argued with them, and what happened to their ideas after Rome.
screen: `BOOK ONE: THANK-YOUS. BOOK TWELVE: GO.` · `STRAIGHT THROUGH: A PERSON, NOT QUOTES.` · `ANAGIGNŌSKŌ: TO READ, TO KNOW AGAIN.` · `NOT FINISHED: START OVER.` · then, large: `READ IT AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath settle. Think back over these weeks of the notebook. One passage probably stuck: the morning warning, the inner retreat, all is opinion, the small share of time, the actor leaving the stage. Pick the one that comes first. If you have the book or a note nearby, find it and read it once, slowly. If not, say it to yourself in your own words. Notice what it means to you today that it didn't the first time. The bell holds the time.
Meditations close. Twelve books of a private notebook, read straight through, from thank-yous to a peaceful exit. Closed, not finished. Today's word.
Your line: read it again. Choose your favorite passage as a morning reading for the coming week, and open it once each day before the phone. Day six hundred forty.

original.note: Greek: to read; built from ana (again) and gignōskō (to know). To read is to know again.
